text: You run a lemonade stand. Each lemonade costs five dollars. Customers line up and pay one at a time, with a five, a ten, or a twenty dollar bill. You have to give correct change, so each customer pays five dollars in the end. You start with no change at all. Return true if you can give every customer correct change.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only have the bills that earlier customers gave me. I can't borrow from a customer who is still in line. So the order of the bills matters, and I must be able to pay change at every step, not just in total. Is that right?
Yes. Change has to be paid right away, with what you have right now.

Okay. One more observation. Change only ever comes in two shapes. A ten needs five back. A twenty needs fifteen back, which is either ten plus five, or three fives. I never hand out a twenty, so I don't need to count twenties at all — just fives and tens. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to ten to the fifth bills, and every bill is a five, a ten, or a twenty.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand customers, so I want one pass. Let me run through the example: five, five, five, ten, twenty. The first three pay with fives, so I hold three fives. The fourth pays ten — I give one five back, so now I have two fives and one ten. The last one pays twenty — I give back the ten and a five. Everyone got change, so the answer is true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try both ways of giving change every time a twenty shows up, and search over all the choices. That branches at every twenty, so the number of paths grows exponentially. With up to a hundred thousand customers, that's way too slow. This problem reminds me of a greedy coin choice. The only real decision is at a twenty: ten plus five, or three fives. And I think there's a clear winner. A five is the more useful bill — a five can pay change for a ten and for a twenty, but a ten can only help with a twenty. So when I have a choice, I should spend the less useful bill, the ten, and keep my fives. That turns it into a simple simulation with two counters.

Here's the plan. I keep two counters, pay five and pay ten — the bills in my cash box after each customer. When a five comes in, I just keep it. When a ten comes in, I hand back one five, and fail right away if I've run out. When a twenty comes in, I give a ten plus a five if I have a ten, otherwise three fives — and again, I fail the moment the five counter would go below zero. The invariant is simple: pay five never goes negative after any customer. One thing worth flagging — why give the ten first? Let me walk through that. Take five, five, five, five, then a ten, a twenty, and another ten. Both strategies are the same up to the twenty. At the twenty, the greedy way hands over a ten and a five, and keeps two fives. The other way burns all three fives and keeps a ten. Then the last customer pays a ten and needs a five back — and there's none left. The greedy way survives; the other way fails. Spending the ten never hurts me, because a ten can't do anything a five can't. One more thing worth flagging — I check for failure right away, inside the loop. If I only checked at the very end, then a ten followed by a five would end at zero fives and look fine — but the first customer already got no change. Checking early is a correctness rule here, not a speed trick. There's a trade-off here. I could keep searching over both choices to be one hundred percent safe. But the argument above shows greedy is never worse, and it runs in linear time with constant space. So I'll go with greedy. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up — and I'll talk through it rather than read it line by line. It's one loop over the bills. A five: pay five goes up by one. A ten: I take one off pay five, and if that drops it below zero I return false on the spot; then pay ten goes up. A twenty: if I hold a ten, I spend the ten and one five; otherwise I take three off pay five. Either way, the moment pay five dips below zero, I return false. If the loop finishes, everyone got their change, so I return true. One thing worth flagging — in the twenty branch, if I have a ten but no five, I return false right away. I don't fall back to three fives, because the fallback needs three fives and I have zero. So no way works, and false is correct. Also, the check is strictly below zero, not below or equal. Landing on exactly zero fives is fine — I paid the change, I'm just out of fives now.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use five, five, ten, ten, twenty — the expected output is false. The two fives come in, so pay five is two. The first ten takes a five: one five left, one ten. The second ten takes my last five: zero fives, two tens. Now the key step. The twenty arrives. I hold two tens but zero fives. I hand back a ten, and now I need a five — pay five goes to negative one, which is below zero, so I return false on the spot. That matches. Two tens are no help here — fifteen dollars of change always needs at least one five. Let's also test with corner cases. A single five: true, no change needed. A single ten, or a single twenty: false — the first customer must pay with a five. A ten then a five: false — that's the case where an end-only check would wrongly say true; my code fails at the first customer. A five then a ten: true — pay five lands exactly on zero, which is why the check is strictly below zero. Three fives then a twenty: true — there's no ten, so the three-fives branch runs. And a hundred thousand fives: true — the counter tops out at one hundred thousand, which fits in an int easily.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear: I look at each bill once, and each step is a few constant-time updates. The space complexity is constant — just two counters, no matter how long the line is. In the worst case every customer can be paid, so the loop runs all the way through before returning true; any failure only makes it stop earlier. Oh, one more thing — the greedy choice is the only smart part, so it's the part I'd test hardest. The easy check is to compare it against the brute force from earlier, the one that tries both ways at every twenty, on lots of short inputs.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that only fives and tens matter, and that the order of customers matters. You proved give-the-ten-first with a real counterexample, instead of just saying greedy. And you showed the early return is about correctness, not speed — plus why the check is strictly below zero, not below or equal. Good work.
